name: Blockchain Definition
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: So What, Precisely, Is a Blockchain?
lesson.summary: A blockchain is a specific way of building a distributed ledger: transactions are grouped into blocks, each block is cryptographically linked to the one before it, and the resulting append-only chain is replicated and independently verified across many nodes.
lesson.body:
With the pieces from the last few sections in hand, a blockchain can finally be defined precisely rather than loosely. A blockchain is a distributed ledger in which data is grouped into batches called blocks, each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, and the resulting chain is held and verified by many independent nodes rather than one central authority. Every word in that sentence is load bearing, and dropping any one of them describes something else entirely.

Take away the distributed ledger part and you have a hash chain sitting on one server, which is a legitimate way to make a local log tamper-evident, but it offers no protection against the one operator who controls that server simply rewriting it and nobody else being able to tell. Take away the hash chain linking and you have a distributed database where independent nodes each hold data, which is useful, but past entries could be edited by whoever controls enough of the network without leaving the specific, chained fingerprint evidence a hash chain provides. Take away immutability, meaning allow the accepted, buried history to be freely rewritten, and you no longer have a record anyone can rely on regardless of how it is structured. A blockchain is specifically the combination: chained blocks, replicated across a network, kept practically unchangeable once accepted.

A useful way to picture the shape: imagine a stack of index cards, where each new card, before it is added to the top of the stack, has a line written on it that is a unique fingerprint of the card directly beneath it. Anyone can pick up the whole stack and verify it is intact by recalculating each fingerprint and checking it against what the card above recorded. If a card in the middle were secretly swapped for a different one, every fingerprint above it, all the way to the top, would fail to match. Now imagine a thousand people each keep their own stack, built by watching the same events and adding cards in the same order, and comparing stacks with each other regularly. That is a blockchain, minus a great deal of cryptographic and networking detail this course will fill in.

It matters to be this specific because the word "blockchain" gets applied loosely to almost any system that touches cryptography or decentralization, including some that are neither distributed nor structured as a chain of blocks at all. A private database with a hash column added to each row is not a blockchain just because someone calls it one. The definition here is not pedantry for its own sake, it is the difference between a system that actually delivers the tamper-evidence and censorship-resistance blockchain is known for, and one that borrows the vocabulary without the architecture.

The chapters ahead take this definition apart piece by piece, starting with what is actually inside a block, how the very first block in a chain gets created with nothing to point back to, and how individual transactions are packaged, signed, and validated before they ever become part of a block.
